# Introduction

Melt of the seasonal snowpack supports over two billion people worldwide by sustaining downstream ecosystems, energy production, and agricultural irrigation [@Immerzeel2020; @Viviroli2020; @Mankin2015]. The high albedo and energy required to melt snow also provides a large-scale cooling effect for the Earth by reflecting most of the incoming solar radiation and dissipating energy during spring melt [@Male1980; @Henderson2018; @Cai2025; @Leach2014]. Snow falls in forested areas over 50% of the northern hemisphere [@Kim2017], and 23% of the global landmass [@Deschamps-Berger2025], where the quantity, timing, and phase of precipitation reaching the ground is altered through snow interception and canopy snow ablation processes. Needleleaf forest canopies can intercept large fractions of snowfall [@Hedstrom1998; @Storck2002], where snow is subjected to greater energy fluxes from increased surface area, longwave irradiance, turbulence, and solar radiation leading to higher rates of sublimation and melt [@Storck2002; @Pomeroy1998b; @Pomeroy2009] compared to the subcanopy snowpack. In cold-dry continental climates, researchers estimate that 25 to 60% of annual snowfall may be lost to the sublimation of intercepted snow from the canopy [@Essery2003; @Sanmiguel-Vallelado2017;@Pomeroy1995; @Ellis2010]. In warm-humid maritime climates the majority of snowfall melts in the canopy [@Storck2002; @Floyd2012], limiting atmospheric losses from sublimation, and contributes to changes in the phase and timing of precipitation reaching the ground. The strong influence of forest canopies on snowfall partitioning leads to a high variability of snowpack accumulation in forested basins [@Rojas-Heredia2024; @Staines2023; @Mazzotti2021; @Moeser2015]. However, observations of this variability are sparse and unrepresentative due to instrumented stations being primarily located in clearing and low elevations [@Vionnet2021]. Moreover, observing snow accumulation under forest canopies over large extents remains limited with current remote sensing methodologies due to the physical interference of forest canopies with electromagnetic radiation [@Rittger2020]. Therefore, accurately quantifying snow accumulation within forested environments requires robust models of snow interception and subsequent ablation processes.

Limited observations of snow interception and canopy snow ablation processes—including throughfall, interception, and the subsequent unloading, wind redistribution, sublimation, drip, and melt of intercepted snow—have led to uncertainties in representing these processes in hydrological models [@Lundquist2021]. Existing snow interception parameterisations have been developed for both warm maritime [@Storck2002; @Andreadis2009] and cold continental [@Hedstrom1998; @Ellis2010; @Roesch2001] climates characterized by dense forest canopy. The strong dependence of snowfall interception and partitioning by forest canopies on meteorology and canopy density [@Hedstrom1998; @Storck2002] has led to differing process emergence in these two distinct climates and forest types and uncertain transferability to new regions [@Lundquist2021; @Lumbrazo2022]. In addition to climate-driven process differences, variability in the measurements used to develop existing theories of snow interception and canopy snow ablation—and uncertainty regarding which processes these measurements capture—also leads to differences in the processes represented in current models. As a result, these parameterisations often need to be calibrated when applied to new regions to better represent local interception processes [e.g., @Lumbrazo2022]. Although satisfactory model performance in simulating subcanopy snow water equivalent (SWE) has been achieved across different climates in some studies [@Essery2004; @Gelfan2004], other snow model comparisons [@Krinner2018; @Rutter2009] have shown limited performance. Moreover, few studies have tested these theories under varying canopy densities and meteorological conditions leading to uncertainty about their applicability across different climates and forest types. 

In hydrological models, the partitioning of snowfall by forest canopies is typically handled by first calculating the fraction of snowfall that is intercepted in the canopy (initial interception) with the remaining fraction attributed to throughfall—the portion of snowfall that passes through gaps in the canopy [@Clark2015; @Pomeroy2022; @Verseghy2017]. Next, ablation of intercepted snow is calculated using parameterisations for processes including unloading, drip, and sublimation [@Ellis2010; @Clark2015; @Pomeroy2022]. @Lundquist2021 and @Staines2023 show that the parameterisations developed by @Hedstrom1998 and @Storck2002, which are commonly used in hydrological and land surface models [@Clark2015; @Pomeroy2022; @Verseghy2017], may overemphasize the effect of canopy snow load and/or air temperature on throughfall during the initial interception process. New observations of initial interception that minimize the inclusion of subsequent canopy snow ablation processes could help determine if existing relationships are generally applicable across a wide range of snow loads and meteorological conditions. Advances in aerial lidar (light detection and ranging) technologies have enabled the creation of highly detailed canopy models [@Staines2023; @Moeser2015]; however, so far, measurements of the interception process at comparable resolutions remain limited to a single site with a dense canopy [@Staines2023]. Moreover, the theory proposed by @Hedstrom1998 to represent variability in initial interception based on snowfall trajectory angle has not yet been validated, and new lidar-derived canopy models offer the potential to do so. Additional observations spanning both meteorological and canopy density gradients would improve assessment of the applicability of existing theories to represent the initial interception process across diverse climates and forest types.

The importance of representing both dry/cold- and melt-induced unloading of snow in the canopy has been shown in several studies [@Gelfan2004; @Essery2004; @Roesch2001; @Ellis2010]. These processes are supported through physical mechanisms such as loss of structural integrity, particle bond weakening, and lubrication of intercepted snow during the melt process [@Storck2002; @Floyd2012]. Sublimation has been proposed to promote unloading via structural degradation and bond weakening of intercepted snow [@MacDonald2010]. Wind drag promotes unloading through shear stress applied to intercepted snow, wind erosion through direct entrainment in the atmosphere of intercepted snow, and branch movement [@Roesch2001; @Bartlett2015; @Lumbrazo2022]. Increasing air temperature promotes unloading by increasing the elasticity of branches and its direct effect on enthalpy and hence melt and/or sublimation [@Schmidt1990; @Schmidt1991]. While direct measurements of canopy snow unloading associated with melt were provided by @Storck2002 from a warm maritime climate using detailed process-level lysimetry, dry-snow unloading parameterisations have only been developed from indirect measurements of above-canopy albedo, which may overestimate unloading because they also capture other ablation processes such as sublimation and melt [@Roesch2001; @Bartlett2015]. Therefore, validation of the theories underlying dry-snow unloading parameterisations would benefit from additional direct observations of canopy snow unloading that are less likely to mix other processes compared to previous indirect measurements. Moreover, the melt-induced unloading relationship proposed by @Storck2002 was based on a single event in a coastal climate and thus should be validated using additional observations across differing meteorologies and canopy snow loads. Additional processes not currently represented in snow interception models—including wind redistribution of snow, rain on intercepted snow, ice deposition, and the cohesion and adhesion of snow within the canopy—should be investigated to assess their relative importance and potential emergence at new sites.

Future climate and land cover changes are expected to change the dominant hydrological processes in forested basins as a result of the dependence of many hydrological processes on temperature, precipitation, and vegetation [@He2021; @He2023; @Dettinger2014; @Viviroli2011; @Fang2020b]. A report by Environment and Climate Change Canada [@Bush2019], suggest an increase in the Canada's mean annual air temperature of 2°C from the 1986-2005 reference period by 2050 for the low emission scenario and 6°C for the high emission scenario by the late 21^st^ century. @Bush2019 project an increase in annual mean precipitation over all of Canada during the second half of the 21^st^ century, with a larger increase in northern Canada. As the climate warms, forest regions across Canada are expected to experience a shift in snow interception processes. For example, continental climates in Canada may shift from a dry-snow unloading- and sublimation-dominated regime to one characterized by increased canopy snowmelt and drip, altering net snow accumulation in these areas. However, the limited transferability of existing parameterisations to inform hydrological predictions resulting from this shift across differing environments makes accurate predictions of these projected changes uncertain. In addition to climate-driven shifts in snow processes, vegetation cover is already changing around the globe due to drought [@Dai2013], disease [@Ruess2021], insect outbreaks [@Kurz2008], fire [@Kasischke2006; @Kasischke2010], land-use change [@Lopez-Moreno2014], and shifts in species composition [@Gottfried2012]. These changes in temperature, precipitation, and forest structure, species, and density are expected to strongly influence snowpack accumulation worldwide. Thus, further investigation into the theories underlying existing snow interception and canopy snow ablation parameterisations is warranted to ensure models of these processes are robust across diverse climates and forest canopies for understanding potential future changes in hydrology worldwide.

To assess the performance of snow interception and canopy snow ablation parameterisations, a modular and flexible model platform will be used to simulate the individual mass and energy balance fluxes and states of the canopy and snowpack. The advantage of modular and flexible model platforms is that it is possible to adjust process parameterisations while holding the remaining model parameters and mass and energy conservation equations constant [@Pomeroy2007; @Clark2015]. The Cold Regions Hydrological Model platform [CRHM, @Pomeroy2022] will be used in this study as its mass and energy balance parameterisations have been successfully used in previous studies [@Ellis2010; @Pomeroy2012; @Rasouli2019b; @Sanmiguel-Vallelado2022] to assess forest-snow interactions in Spain, USA, and Canada. Since CRHM is a process-based model agnostic platform, individual state and flux variables including subcanopy snow accumulation, snow interception, sublimation, unloading, drip, and wind redistribution can be evaluated using differing parameterisations. To evaluate existing parameterisations of snow interception [@Hedstrom1998;@Storck2002;@Andreadis2009], and ablation of canopy snow by unloading [@Ellis2010; @Roesch2001; @Andreadis2009], drip [@Storck2002;@Andreadis2009; @Ellis2010] and sublimation [@Pomeroy1998b], CRHM will be run at four mountain forest research basins in western and northern Canada and compared to in-situ observations of subcanopy SWE. Modifications to the existing parameterisations to improve representation of snow interception processes based on field investigations at a well instrumented subalpine forest in the Canadian Rockies will be validated on the associated change in error in simulated and observed forest snow accumulation and other interception processes where measured.

## Research Objectives

This study aims to improve understanding of processes that govern snow interception and canopy snow ablation, and determine how these processes can be accurately represented in hydrological models applicable across a range of climate and forest types. To achieve this goal, two specific research objectives were formulated each with underlying research questions:

### Objective 1: Evaluate the suitability of existing snow interception and ablation theories and advance process understanding across a broad range of canopy densities and meteorological conditions.

1. What are the theoretical underpinnings and assumptions underlying existing snow interception and ablation parameterisations?  
   
2. To what extent are the process assumptions of existing parameterisations supported by in-situ measurements collected across diverse canopy structures and meteorological conditions?  
   
3. How can improved understanding of snow interception and ablation processes inform a more accurate representation of these processes in a hydrological model?

### Objective 2: Determine how new snow interception and ablation parameterisations could enhance simulation of canopy and subcanopy snow storage, and diagnose the causative processes governing snow accumulation in needleleaf forests. 

4. How can the use of novel snow interception and ablation parameterisations improve simulations of snow storage within and beneath forest canopies with differing tree species, canopy structures, and climate?

5. What are the dominant processes that control the partitioning of intercepted snow into sublimation, drip, and unloading and account for differences in subcanopy snow accumulation across forests with diverse vegetation and climatic conditions?

## Organization of Chapters

Following the Introduction (Chapter 1), four manuscripts are presented as thesis chapters designed for submission to peer-reviewed journals and to address the objectives and corresponding research questions. Chapter 2 addresses Research Question 1 by providing a comprehensive review of the literature on snow interception and canopy snow ablation parameterisations. This review identified the fundamental theories and assumptions underlying existing parameterisations and highlights the primary research gaps that this thesis seeks to address.

Chapter 3 addresses the initial snow interception component of both Research Questions 2 and 3. As part of Research Question 2, the process assumptions underlying existing initial snow interception parameterisations are evaluated using new observations. To address part of Research Question 3, new parameterisations are presented and evaluated across a broad range of canopy densities and meteorological conditions.

Chapter 4 addresses the remaining components of Research Question 2 and 3 regarding the evaluation and development of canopy snow ablation parameterisations. Observed relationships of canopy snow ablation and meteorology are evaluated and compared against existing theories to address Research Question 2. The chapter also presents an evaluation of a new canopy snow energy and mass balance parameterisations, addressing the second part of Research Question 3. Collectively, Chapters 2 through 4 demonstrate the successful completion of Objective 1 and its associated research questions.

Chapter 5 addresses Research Question 4 of Objective 2 by implementing the new canopy snow energy and mass balance parameterisations—developed in Chapters 3 and 4—within the Cold Regions Hydrological Modelling Platform and evaluating them at four research sites in western and northern Canada. At each site, the dominant processes controlling the partitioning of intercepted snow are also identified, thereby addressing Research Question 5. 

The thesis concludes with Chapter 6, which summarises how the research gaps have been addressed, highlights the contributions of this work to the discipline, and outlines its limitations and directions for future research.
